title: Rasch Measurement Explorations
text:
Preface
This book collects the simulation studies and methods notes written while developing the R package easyRasch2. Each chapter starts from a question that came up when choosing a default, a cutoff or a statistic for the package, and reports what the simulations showed. Most of them will never become journal articles, but the results are useful beyond the package, and they should be possible to find, check and cite.

title: Rasch Measurement Explorations
text:
How the chapters work
Every chapter is self-contained and can be read on its own. Where one study depends on another, the dependency is a cross-reference to that chapter.
Each chapter opens with a box giving its status, the easyRasch2 and R versions it was computed with, and a suggested citation. The status is one of:

Complete. The study answers its question and the results are not expected to change.
Preliminary. The design is settled, but parts are still running or being checked.
Superseded. A later chapter replaces it, and the box says which.

The dates under each chapter title are when it was first published and last modified. A revision that changes a result is listed in the chapter’s revision history, with what changed and why. Edits to wording are not listed. The full history of every chapter is in the GitHub repository, linked from the “View source” button on each page.

The code that produces each table and figure is in the chapter, folded by default. Simulations that take more than a few minutes do not run when the book is built. They are in the scripts/ folder of the repository, one subfolder per topic, and the chapter says which script produced which result. Some chapters call internal easyRasch2 functions with easyRasch2:::. These are not part of the package’s public interface and may change between versions.

title: 1  Calibration of the asymptotic item-restscore test
text:
1.1 Purpose
RMitemRestscore() flags items using the p-value from iarm::item_restscore(). The test statistic is
\[
z_i = \frac{\hat\gamma_i^{\text{obs}} - \hat\gamma_i^{\text{exp}}}{\text{ASE}(\hat\gamma_i^{\text{obs}})},
\]
referred to the standard normal, two-sided, then adjusted over the \(k\) items (BH by default). The observed gamma is Goodman-Kruskal gamma for the item × restscore table. The expected gamma is computed from the CML item parameters and the observed score distribution. The ASE is the delta-method standard error that vcdExtra::GKgamma() returns for the observed table.
Two features of this construction give reasons to check calibration directly instead of assuming it:
The partial gamma LD and DIF functions already have simulation-based cutoffs. Item-restscore does not. RMitemRestscoreBoot() resamples the data and counts how often each item is flagged, which describes stability and not calibration.
An earlier simulation hinted at this. It reported item-restscore as well calibrated from per-item false positive rates, but counted as the share of replications with at least one BH-flagged item, its small-sample rate was above 5 percent. That study is not reported here, so this is the motivation for the check, not evidence.

title: 1  Calibration of the asymptotic item-restscore test
text:
The expected gamma is treated as known. It is a function of estimated thresholds, and it is estimated from the same data as the observed gamma. The ASE ignores both the estimation uncertainty and the correlation between the two terms. The sign of the resulting bias cannot be worked out without simulating it.
The ASE is the delta-method SE computed under the alternative. van der Ark and van Aert (2015) found it had the worst coverage of four CI types for bivariate gamma, but only for tables up to 5 × 5 at N ≤ 100 (van der Ark & van Aert, 2015). The item × restscore table is larger (4 × 28 for nine four-category items), with sparse cells in the tails of the restscore.

title: 1  Calibration of the asymptotic item-restscore test
text:
1.2 Design

Item sets. (a) 20 dichotomous items with locations evenly spaced on [-2, 2], as in the S-X2 comparison (Section 2.3.1). (b) 9 polytomous items with four categories, locations evenly spaced on [-1.5, 1.5], and thresholds at location ± 1.2 and location + 0, as a PHQ-9-sized scale.
Persons. θ ~ N(μ, 1.5²), with μ = 0 (targeted) or μ = 1.5 (mistargeted), since sparse restscore tails are a plausible source of miscalibration.
Sample sizes. 150, 300, 600, 1000, 2000.
Replications. 4000 per cell. The Monte Carlo SE of a 5 percent rate is then 0.34 points.
Fitting. Same as the package: psychotools::pcmodel(), then iarm::item_restscore(). A replication with an unobserved category (or an item with zero variance) is discarded and counted, since the package would not fit it either.

iarm returns its results rounded to four decimals, so \(z\) is recomputed from the rounded observed, expected and SE columns and the p-values from \(z\). With SEs around .02 to .05 the rounding moves \(z\) by at most about .003.
For each item and replication the observed gamma, expected gamma and ASE are stored. Calibration is summarised in three ways.

Per-item rejection at two-sided α = .05, and separately in each tail at .025.
Family-wise rejection (any item flagged) with no adjustment, BH as in the package default, and Bonferroni.
A decomposition of the SE. If the ASE were correct for the test statistic, the empirical SD of \(\hat\gamma^{\text{obs}} - \hat\gamma^{\text{exp}}\) across replications would equal the root mean squared ASE. The ratio \(\text{SD}(\hat\gamma^{\text{obs}}) / \text{RMS(ASE)}\) checks the ASE as an SE for the observed gamma alone. Comparing the two ratios separates point 1 from point 2 in Section 1.1.

1.2.2 Data generation
Partial credit model, vectorised over persons. thr is one threshold vector per item. A dichotomous item is a PCM item with one threshold.


Code
sim_pcm <- function(theta, thr) {
  n <- length(theta)
  sapply(thr, function(d) {
    m <- length(d)
    eta <- outer(theta, 0:m) -
      matrix(c(0, cumsum(d)), n, m + 1, byrow = TRUE)
    p <- exp(eta - apply(eta, 1, max))
    p <- p / rowSums(p)
    cp <- p %*% upper.tri(diag(m + 1), diag = TRUE)
    rowSums(runif(n) > cp)
  })
}




1.2.3 One replication


Code
one_rep <- function(rep, set, n, mu) {
  set.seed(1e7 * match(set, names(item_sets)) + 1e5 * match(mu, MUS) +
             10 * n + rep)
  thr <- item_sets[[set]]
  d <- as.data.frame(sim_pcm(rnorm(n, mu, THETA_SD), thr))
  names(d) <- paste0("I", seq_along(thr))

  # every category observed in every item, as the CML fit requires
  full <- all(mapply(function(x, m) all(tabulate(x + 1, m + 1) > 0),
                     d, lengths(thr)))
  if (!full) return(NULL)

  res <- tryCatch({
    fit <- psychotools::pcmodel(d, hessian = FALSE)
    r <- iarm::item_restscore(fit, p.adj = "none")
    matrix(as.numeric(r[seq_along(thr), c("observed", "expected", "se")]),
           ncol = 3, dimnames = list(NULL, c("obs", "exp", "se")))
  }, error = function(e) NULL)
  res
}




1.2.4 Run
Results are cached. Delete results/restscore/restscore_asymptotic_null.rds to force a re-run.

if (file.exists(RES_FILE)) {
  sim <- readRDS(RES_FILE)
} else {
  t0 <- Sys.time()
  res <- mclapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)),
                  function(i) one_rep(grid$rep[i], grid$set[i],
                                      grid$n[i], grid$mu[i]),
                  mc.cores = NCORES, mc.preschedule = TRUE)
  sim <- list(res = res, grid = grid, item_sets = item_sets,
              elapsed_min = as.numeric(Sys.time() - t0, units = "mins"))

title: 1  Calibration of the asymptotic item-restscore test
text:
1.4 Interpretation
The asymptotic item-restscore test is not calibrated. Two separate distortions act on it, and neither vanishes as n grows.
1. The ASE is right for the observed gamma but wrong for the test statistic. The SD of the observed gamma across replications matches the root mean squared ASE to within 1 percent in every cell, so the delta-method SE is not the problem. The problem is that the expected gamma varies across samples and moves with the observed gamma (correlation about .41 for the dichotomous set and .55 for the polytomous set). Its variance roughly equals the covariance, so the difference varies less than the observed gamma alone. The SD of the difference is 0.91 times the ASE for dichotomous items and 0.83 times for polytomous items, nearly constant across sample size and targeting. Dividing by the ASE therefore shrinks \(z\) by a fixed factor, and the test is conservative at every sample size. This is point 1 from Section 1.1, and point 2 does not show up at all.
2. A small-sample bias pushes \(z\) upwards. Mean \(z\) is .15 at n = 150 and falls to .04 at n = 2000, roughly in proportion to \(1/\sqrt{n}\). This is what a bias of order \(1/n\) in the gamma difference produces. It inflates the upper tail (observed gamma above expected, labelled overfit by the package) and depletes the lower tail. It is largest for items far from the person mean, reaching 14 percent two-sided at n = 150 for the easiest dichotomous item under mistargeting.
Net effect on single items. Nominal is 5 percent two-sided. Dichotomous items reject 4.7 percent at n = 150 when targeted, falling to 3.1 at n = 2000. Polytomous items reject 2.9 falling to 1.9. The tails are lopsided. The lower tail, which is the underfit direction and the usual signature of multidimensionality, rejects 0.2 to 1.2 percent against a nominal 2.5 in every cell, a tenth to a half of what it should. The upper tail exceeds 2.5 percent at small n for dichotomous items. The power cost of the deflated lower tail is not measured here, but it follows directly: underfit has to be larger than the nominal level implies before it is flagged.
Family-wise rates, which is what a user sees. With BH over the items, the probability that a true Rasch model gets at least one item flagged is:

dichotomous, targeted: 13.5, 6.2, 4.1, 2.7 and 2.3 percent at n = 150 to 2000
dichotomous, mistargeted: 30.5, 13.9, 7.4, 4.9 and 3.2 percent
polytomous, targeted: 4.2 falling to 0.9 to 1.1 percent
polytomous, mistargeted: 5.1 falling to 1.2 to 1.6 percent

So the same test is liberal for dichotomous data at small n, especially when mistargeted, and conservative for polytomous data at every n. No single correction to the nominal level fixes both. BH and Bonferroni give nearly identical rates, as expected under a complete null.
Discarded replications. 28 percent of the mistargeted polytomous replications at n = 150 and 6 percent at n = 300 had an unobserved category and were discarded. Those two cells describe samples where every category is used, which are also the only samples the package can fit.
For easyRasch2. Both distortions come from treating the expected gamma as a fixed reference, and both depend on the item set, sample size and targeting. A parametric bootstrap that simulates from the fitted model, re-estimates the thresholds in every replication, and recomputes the observed minus expected difference would absorb both, in the same way as RMitemInfitCutoff(). A bootstrap that holds the thresholds fixed would reproduce distortion 1. The item-restscore statistic is cheap (about 0.1 s per replication including the CML fit), so an RMitemRestscoreCutoff() at the same iteration counts as the infit cutoffs is affordable. This simulation says nothing about power. That comparison, against infit with simulation-based cutoffs, is the natural next step.

title: 2  Generalized S-X2 and conditional infit
text:
2.1 Purpose
Conditional infit with simulation-based cutoffs detects misfit well, but when several items misfit and the sample is large it also flags many items that fit, a cascade documented by Johansson (2025). The generalized S-X2 index (Kang & Chen, 2008; Orlando & Thissen, 2000) is a natural candidate for a complement. It compares observed and expected proportions within sum-score groups, and Kang & Chen (2008) report nominal Type I error from n = 500 to n = 5000. Two features of that literature leave the question open. Power was evaluated only where every item misfit, and the follow-up on the graded response model found power “much lower when the source of misfit was multidimensionality” (Kang & Chen, 2011), which is the misfit that matters most in applied Rasch analysis.
This chapter first checks whether S-X2 holds its nominal level under a true Rasch model (Section 2.2), finds that it does not and why, and then compares calibrated versions of S-X2 with conditional infit on the same datasets, with every method held to a family-wise error rate (Section 2.3).
Every replication in both studies generates new data. Designs that draw every replication from one large simulated dataset leave each sample unbiased but make the replications dependent, so their Monte Carlo SEs are too small and differences between sample sizes can be noise from that one dataset.

section: 2.2 S-X2 under a true Rasch model
text:
2.2 S-X2 under a true Rasch model

2.2.1 The degrees of freedom
mirt computes the degrees of freedom of S-X2 for each item as the number of score groups left after collapsing sparse cells, minus the item’s own parameters, minus every estimated latent parameter. For itemtype = "Rasch" the latent variance is estimated, so each item loses one degree of freedom that the definition of Orlando & Thissen (2000) does not remove. The variance acts as a slope shared by all items, and charging it to every item counts it once per item. The deduction is deliberate: mirt’s NEWS lists it under version 1.20.1 as a df adjustment “for models where the latent trait hyper-parameters have been estimated”.
If S-X2 follows a chi-square distribution on df + 1 and is referred to df, the rejection rate at .05 is 7.5 percent at df = 10 and 6.9 percent at df = 17, the range of df that 20 dichotomous items give between n = 150 and 2000.


2.2.2 Design

Item sets. 20 dichotomous items evenly spaced on [-2, 2]. 20 dichotomous items at clustered locations from a single runif(20, -2, 2) draw (seed 20250727), to check that the result does not depend on even spacing. Nine items with four categories, locations evenly spaced on [-1.5, 1.5], thresholds at location -1.2, 0 and +1.2.
Persons. \(\theta \sim N(0, 1.5^2)\).
Sample sizes. 150, 500 and 2000, with 2000 replications per cell. The Monte Carlo SE of a 5 percent rate is about 0.5 points.

Four variants of S-X2, from at most two fits per replication:








Variant
Fit
Reference




V0
Rasch, variance estimated
chi-square on mirt’s df


V1
same as V0
chi-square on df + 1


V2
same as V0, mincell = 5
mirt’s df, and df + 1 (V2c)


V3
Rasch, variance fixed at the true 2.25
mirt’s df, which then has no latent deduction



V1 tests the df. V3 removes the deduction and the estimation error in the variance together, so comparing V1 with V3 separates the two. V2 tests stricter collapsing of sparse score groups. The simulation is scripts/sx2/sx2_null_diagnostic.R. No replication was discarded.


Code
dg <- readRDS("results/sx2/null_diagnostic.rds")
dg_ok <- !vapply(dg$res, is.null, logical(1))
dg_long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(which(dg_ok), function(i) {
  g <- dg$grid[i, ]; m <- dg$res[[i]]
  data.frame(set = g$set, n = g$n, rep = g$rep, item = seq_len(nrow(m)), m)
})) |>
  mutate(p_v1  = pchisq(S_v0, df_v0 + 1, lower.tail = FALSE),
         p_v2c = pchisq(S_v2, df_v2 + 1, lower.tail = FALSE),
         set = factor(set, levels = c("dich_even", "dich_orig", "poly"),
                      labels = c("20 dichotomous, even", "20 dichotomous, clustered",
                                 "9 items, 4 categories")))

dg_p <- dg_long |>
  select(set, n, rep, item, V0 = p_v0, V1 = p_v1, V2 = p_v2, V2c = p_v2c,
         V3 = p_v3) |>
  pivot_longer(V0:V3, names_to = "variant", values_to = "p")

v_col <- c(V0 = "#4a3aa7", V1 = "#eb6834", V3 = "#eb6834")
v_lty <- c(V0 = "solid", V1 = "solid", V3 = "dashed")
v_shp <- c(V0 = 18, V1 = 17, V3 = 2)
v_lab <- c(V0 = "mirt df (V0)", V1 = "df + 1 (V1)", V3 = "variance fixed (V3)")

variant_plot <- function(d, ylab, band = NULL) {
  p <- ggplot(d, aes(factor(n), v, colour = variant, linetype = variant,
                     shape = variant, group = variant))
  if (!is.null(band)) {
    p <- p + annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 5 - band,
                      ymax = 5 + band, fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.6)
  }
  p +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(size = 2.2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = v_col, labels = v_lab, name = NULL) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = v_lty, labels = v_lab, name = NULL) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = v_shp, labels = v_lab, name = NULL) +
    facet_wrap(~ set) +
    labs(x = "Sample size", y = ylab) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}




2.2.3 Per-item rejection


Code
dg_p |>
  filter(variant %in% c("V0", "V1", "V3")) |>
  group_by(set, variant, n) |>
  summarise(v = 100 * mean(p < .05, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  variant_plot("Items rejected at .05 (%)") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 10), breaks = seq(0, 10, 2))








Figure 2.1: Per-item rejection rate of S-X2 at .05 under a true Rasch model, 2000 datasets per sample size. The dashed horizontal line is the nominal 5 percent. The two variants with one more degree of freedom than mirt’s default overlap.





Adding the missing degree of freedom brings every cell to nominal: V1 rejects 4.8 to 5.3 percent of items against 6.0 to 7.5 under V0. V1 and V3 agree to within 0.2 points in every cell, so estimating the latent variance costs nothing and the df is the whole of the per-item excess. Under mirt’s df, S-X2 exceeds its df by 0.96 to 1.07 on average for dichotomous items, and with the variance fixed the mean excess is within 0.07 of zero (Table 2.1). The polytomous set shows the same pattern from n = 500. At n = 150 its excess is 1.66 under V0 and 0.64 under V3, so something else adds to the statistic there.
Stricter collapsing on its own (V2) is worse than the default, because mincell = 5 merges so many score groups at n = 150 that the df falls to about 2, and a one-df shortfall weighs more at small df. With the df corrected (V2c) it is close to nominal for dichotomous items, but at n = 150 it leaves too few score groups to say much (Table 2.2).


2.2.4 The far tail and the family-wise rate
BH over 20 items rejects on p-values near \(.05 / 20\), so the family-wise rate depends on the far tail of the p-value distribution, not on its 5 percent point.


Code
dg_p |>
  filter(variant %in% c("V0", "V1", "V3")) |>
  group_by(set, variant, n, rep) |>
  summarise(any = any(p.adjust(p, "BH") < .05, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(set, variant, n) |>
  summarise(v = 100 * mean(any), .groups = "drop") |>
  variant_plot("Datasets with any BH flag (%)",
               band = 100 * 2 * sqrt(.05 * .95 / 2000)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 14), breaks = seq(0, 14, 2))








Figure 2.2: Share of datasets with at least one item flagged by S-X2 with BH under a true Rasch model, 2000 datasets per sample size. The band covers two Monte Carlo SEs around 5 percent.





Correcting the df leaves part of the problem. Under V1, items reach p < .005 at 6.4 to 7.7 per 1000 for dichotomous items against a nominal 5, and BH flags at least one item in 6.8 to 8.6 percent of datasets. That is down from 10.7 to 12.5 under V0 but still above 5. The polytomous set is close to nominal under V1, at 4.3 to 6.5 percent. V2c removes the tail excess for dichotomous items (3.4 to 5.3 per 1000 and 3.6 to 5.9 percent family-wise), which points to sparse score groups as the source of what remains (Table 2.3, Table 2.4). None of the rates rises steadily with sample size.

title: 2  Generalized S-X2 and conditional infit
text:
2.3 S-X2 against conditional infit

2.3.1 Design

Items. 20 dichotomous items, locations evenly spaced on [-2, 2].
Persons. A bivariate normal, both dimensions SD 1.5, correlation \(\rho\). Fitting items respond to the first dimension, misfitting items to the second.
Misfit. k = 1 misfitting item (nearest 0 logits) or k = 3 (nearest 0, -1 and -2). \(\rho\) = 0.15 is strong multidimensionality, 0.50 and 0.75 are subtle.
Sample sizes. 150, 500, 1000 and 2000. 500 replications in each null cell (k = 0) and 200 in each misfit cell. The Monte Carlo SE of a 5 percent family-wise rate is 1.0 point.








Label
Method




Infit, Westfall-Young
conditional infit, RMitemInfitCutoff() with B = 400, Westfall-Young step-down, the easyRasch2 default


Infit, Holm
same bootstrap, Holm on the marginal p


S-X2, mirt df
chi-square on mirt’s df, Holm


S-X2, df + 1
chi-square on df + 1, Holm


S-X2, df + 1, BH
chi-square on df + 1, BH


S-X2, bootstrap
parametric bootstrap with B = 400 and a refit per draw, Westfall-Young


RMSEA, bootstrap
RMSEA.S_X2 from the same draws, Westfall-Young


RMSEA > .05
a fixed threshold, as is sometimes recommended



Every method is corrected for a family-wise error rate, with Westfall-Young or Holm, except the BH variant. The design written before the run used BH for the asymptotic S-X2 arms. BH controls the false discovery rate instead, and once the misfitting items are rejected it loosens its threshold for the rest, so it flags more fitting items than a family-wise method would. Holm was added after the run from the stored p-values to make the comparison fair, and BH is kept in the appendix tables to show the difference.
The S-X2 bootstrap draws datasets from the fitted Rasch model, refits each and computes S-X2 for every item. The number of score groups changes between draws, so the bootstrap statistic is \(z = \Phi^{-1}(1 - p)\), with \(p\) from the chi-square on df + 1, which is on a common scale whatever the df. It goes through the same Westfall-Young step-down that easyRasch2 uses for infit, so the two arms differ only in the statistic. The design and a decision rule were written before the run. The simulation is scripts/sx2/sx2_comparison.R, about 7.6 hours on 10 cores. Every replication returned results for every method and no bootstrap draw was dropped.


Code
fs <- list.files("results/sx2/comparison", "\\.rds$", full.names = TRUE)
L <- lapply(fs, readRDS)
long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(L, function(x) do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(x$res), function(r) {
  y <- x$res[[r]]
  if (is.null(y$res)) return(NULL)
  cbind(k = x$cell$k, rho = x$cell$rho, n = x$cell$n, rep = r, y$res)
}))))

methods <- c("infit_wy", "infit_holm", "sx2_mirt", "sx2_df1", "sx2_df1_bh",
             "sx2_boot", "rmsea_boot", "rmsea_05")

adj <- long |>
  group_by(k, rho, n, rep) |>
  mutate(infit_wy = padj_infit, infit_holm = p.adjust(p_infit, "holm"),
         sx2_mirt = p.adjust(p_mirt, "holm"), sx2_df1 = p.adjust(p_df1, "holm"),
         sx2_df1_bh = p.adjust(p_df1, "BH"),
         sx2_boot = padj_sx2boot, rmsea_boot = padj_rmseaboot) |>
  ungroup()

flags <- adj |>
  mutate(across(c(infit_wy, infit_holm, sx2_mirt, sx2_df1, sx2_df1_bh, sx2_boot,
                  rmsea_boot),
                \(p) p < .05),
         rmsea_05 = rmsea > .05) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(methods), names_to = "method", values_to = "flag") |>
  mutate(flag = coalesce(flag, FALSE),
         method = factor(method, levels = methods))

pal <- c(infit_wy = "#2a78d6", sx2_df1 = "#eb6834", sx2_boot = "#1baf7a",
         sx2_mirt = "#4a3aa7", rmsea_05 = "grey55")
shp <- c(infit_wy = 16, sx2_df1 = 17, sx2_boot = 15, sx2_mirt = 18,
         rmsea_05 = 4)
lty <- c(infit_wy = "solid", sx2_df1 = "solid", sx2_boot = "solid",
         sx2_mirt = "solid", rmsea_05 = "dashed")
lab <- c(infit_wy = "Infit, Westfall-Young", sx2_df1 = "S-X2, df + 1, Holm",
         sx2_boot = "S-X2, bootstrap", sx2_mirt = "S-X2, mirt df, Holm",
         rmsea_05 = "RMSEA > .05")

cell_lab <- function(d) d |>
  mutate(cell = factor(sprintf("k = %d, rho = %.2f", k, rho),
                       levels = c("k = 1, rho = 0.50", "k = 1, rho = 0.75",
                                  "k = 3, rho = 0.15", "k = 3, rho = 0.50",
                                  "k = 3, rho = 0.75")))

rate_plot <- function(d, ylab, ylim = c(0, 100)) {
  ggplot(d, aes(factor(n), v, colour = method, shape = method,
                linetype = method, group = method)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(size = 2.2) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = pal, labels = lab, name = NULL) +
    scale_shape_manual(values = shp, labels = lab, name = NULL) +
    scale_linetype_manual(values = lty, labels = lab, name = NULL) +
    scale_y_continuous(limits = ylim) +
    labs(x = "Sample size", y = ylab) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom", panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
}

fig_methods <- c("infit_wy", "sx2_df1", "sx2_boot", "rmsea_05")




2.3.2 Under the null


Code
null_fw <- flags |>
  filter(k == 0) |>
  group_by(method, n, rep) |>
  summarise(any = any(flag), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(method, n) |>
  summarise(v = 100 * mean(any), .groups = "drop")

mcse <- 100 * 2 * sqrt(.05 * .95 / 500)
null_fw |>
  filter(method %in% c("infit_wy", "sx2_mirt", "sx2_df1", "sx2_boot")) |>
  rate_plot("Datasets with any flag (%)", ylim = c(0, 14)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = 5 - mcse, ymax = 5 + mcse,
           fill = "grey85", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40")








Figure 2.3: Share of datasets with at least one flagged item under a true Rasch model (k = 0, 500 datasets per n). The band covers two Monte Carlo SEs around 5 percent. RMSEA above .05 is left out, since it flags 99.2 percent of datasets at n = 150.





Infit with Westfall-Young holds 4.2 to 4.4 percent at every n. The S-X2 bootstrap gives 6.2 and 6.6 percent at n = 150 and 500 and 4.8 and 3.8 percent at n = 1000 and 2000. The first two are 1.2 and 1.6 Monte Carlo SEs above 5, so it is at most slightly liberal at small n. Asymptotic S-X2 with Holm gives 5.8 to 8.6 percent with the df corrected, in line with Section 2.2, and 8.6 to 12.0 with mirt’s df. RMSEA above .05 flags almost every dataset at n = 150 and none at n = 2000 (Table 2.5).
RMSEA with a bootstrap cutoff behaves like the S-X2 bootstrap in every cell, as expected, since both come from the same draws and RMSEA is close to a monotone function of S-X2. Infit with Holm on the marginal bootstrap p is close to infit with Westfall-Young and slightly more conservative. Both are left out of the figures and kept in the appendix tables.


2.3.3 Detection of the misfitting items


Code
flags |>
  filter(k > 0, misfit, method %in% fig_methods) |>
  group_by(k, rho, n, method) |>
  summarise(v = 100 * mean(flag), .groups = "drop") |>
  cell_lab() |>
  rate_plot("Detection (%)") +
  facet_wrap(~ cell, nrow = 2)








Figure 2.4: Detection of the misfitting items, averaged over the misfitting items in each dataset. k is the number of misfitting items and rho the correlation between the two dimensions, lower meaning stronger misfit.





Infit with Westfall-Young detects at least as much as the S-X2 bootstrap in every cell, and clearly more wherever detection is not saturated. The gap is largest for subtle misfit. At \(\rho\) = 0.75 it is 80 against 47.5 percent with one misfitting item at n = 500, and 58 against 32 percent with three at n = 1000. The S-X2 bootstrap only catches up where both methods reach 100 percent (Table 2.6).
The fixed RMSEA threshold detects more at n = 150 because it flags almost everything there, and falls to 1.3 percent at \(\rho\) = 0.75 and n = 2000, because the RMSEA of a subtly misfitting item settles below .05 as n grows. With three misfitting items at \(\rho\) = 0.75, their median RMSEA falls from .047 at n = 150 to .031 at n = 2000. A bootstrap cutoff for RMSEA recovers 68.7 percent in the same cell, but no more than the S-X2 bootstrap.


2.3.4 False flags on fitting items


Code
flags |>
  filter(k > 0, !misfit, method %in% fig_methods) |>
  group_by(k, rho, n, method, rep) |>
  summarise(any = any(flag), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(k, rho, n, method) |>
  summarise(v = 100 * mean(any), .groups = "drop") |>
  cell_lab() |>
  rate_plot("Datasets with a fitting item flagged (%)") +
  facet_wrap(~ cell, nrow = 2)








Figure 2.5: Share of datasets in which at least one fitting item is flagged. Panels as in Figure 2.4.





This is where S-X2 differs. With three misfitting items, infit flags fitting items in a share of datasets that rises steeply with n: at \(\rho\) = 0.50, 16 percent at n = 500, 39.5 at 1000 and 87 at 2000. The S-X2 bootstrap stays at 2 to 7.5 percent in the same cells. At \(\rho\) = 0.15 infit flags fitting items in 97 percent of datasets at n = 1000 against 6.5 for the S-X2 bootstrap, and only at n = 2000 does the S-X2 bootstrap also cascade, to 47.5 percent. Counted per item at \(\rho\) = 0.15 and n = 2000, infit flags 57.1 percent of the fitting items and the S-X2 bootstrap 3.7 percent. With a single misfitting item the cascade is milder for infit, up to 21 percent at \(\rho\) = 0.50 and n = 2000, against 5 percent (Table 2.7).
Asymptotic S-X2 with the df corrected and Holm resists the cascade almost as well as the bootstrap. With three misfitting items it flags fitting items in 2.5, 4.5 and 9 percent of datasets at \(\rho\) = 0.50 and n = 500, 1000 and 2000, against 2, 3.5 and 7.5 for the bootstrap, and its detection is as high or slightly higher. With BH the same p-values flag fitting items in 7, 14.5 and 28 percent of datasets, which is the effect of the correction, not of the statistic. Infit with Holm still cascades, to 72.5 percent at \(\rho\) = 0.50 and n = 2000, so the cascade under infit is not a property of Westfall-Young either.
A likely reason is what each statistic is sensitive to. The cascade leaves the fitting items with small deviations in slope relative to the misspecified model. Infit is close to a one-degree-of-freedom contrast in slope, so it picks such deviations up, while S-X2 spreads them over 15 to 17 degrees of freedom at n = 1000 and 2000 and has little power against them.
The fitting items are fitting by construction, since they respond only to the first dimension. In the unidimensional model fitted to the whole set, the misfitting items distort the person locations, so fitting items can show misfit too (Johansson, 2025). Flagging them is a false positive with respect to the data generating model. Multiplicity control does not prevent it, since at large n those items are far outside their null distribution.


2.3.5 Recovering the right items


Code
flags |>
  filter(k > 0, method %in% fig_methods) |>
  group_by(k, rho, n, method, rep) |>
  summarise(v = all(flag[misfit]) & !any(flag[!misfit]), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(k, rho, n, method) |>
  summarise(v = 100 * mean(v), .groups = "drop") |>
  cell_lab() |>
  rate_plot("Perfect recovery (%)") +
  facet_wrap(~ cell, nrow = 2)








Figure 2.6: Share of datasets in which every misfitting item is flagged and no fitting item is. Panels as in Figure 2.4.





The two effects trade off. With three misfitting items the S-X2 bootstrap recovers the right set far more often at n \(\geq\) 1000 when misfit is strong or moderate: 93.5 against 3 percent at \(\rho\) = 0.15 and n = 1000, and 92.5 against 13 percent at \(\rho\) = 0.50 and n = 2000. Infit is better at small n and for subtle misfit, where the S-X2 bootstrap misses too many of the misfitting items: 41.5 against 26.5 percent at \(\rho\) = 0.75 and n = 2000, and 47 against 30 percent at \(\rho\) = 0.50 and n = 500 (Table 2.8).


2.3.6 Detection by item location


Code
flags |>
  filter(k == 3, misfit, rho > 0.15, method %in% c("infit_wy", "sx2_boot")) |>
  mutate(location = factor(sprintf("item at %.2f logits", location),
                           levels = sprintf("item at %.2f logits",
                                            sort(unique(location)))),
         rho = sprintf("rho = %.2f", rho)) |>
  group_by(rho, n, location, method) |>
  summarise(v = 100 * mean(flag), .groups = "drop") |>
  rate_plot("Detection (%)") +
  facet_grid(rho ~ location)








Figure 2.7: Detection of each of the three misfitting items by its location relative to the sample mean, for the two subtler conditions.





Both methods find it hardest to detect the item two logits below the sample mean, and the S-X2 bootstrap loses most relative to infit on the two items closer to the centre at \(\rho\) = 0.75 (Table 2.9).


2.3.7 At a matched null error rate
The S-X2 bootstrap is slightly above 5 percent under the null at small n and infit slightly below, which favours S-X2 in the comparisons above. In Table 2.10 each method’s adjusted p-value threshold is set so that its family-wise rate in the null cell at the same n is 5 percent, and that threshold is applied to the misfit cells. The thresholds come from the same design, so they are an oracle.
Matching the null error rate moves detection by at most 3.3 points. False flags move more where a threshold loosens, by up to 6.5 points for infit and 13.5 for the S-X2 bootstrap, both at \(\rho\) = 0.15, where the cascade is steepest. Infit still detects more in every unsaturated cell, and the S-X2 bootstrap still flags far fewer fitting items when three items misfit.


2.3.8 Paired comparison
Both methods were run on the same datasets, so their decisions can be compared item by item. Table 2.11 counts misfitting items detected by one method and not the other. Where the two disagree about a misfitting item, it is almost always infit that detects it. The largest counts in the other direction, 15 to 17 out of 600, are in cells where infit alone detects 92 to 172.

title: 2  Generalized S-X2 and conditional infit
text:
2.4 Interpretation
1. mirt’s S-X2 is liberal for Rasch models. Subtracting the latent variance from every item’s df makes S-X2 reject 6 to 7.5 percent of items at a nominal 5 under a true Rasch or partial credit model. Adding the df back, or fixing the variance, gives 4.8 to 5.3. Whether the adjustment is right for other models is not tested here.
2. Correcting the df is not enough for a family of dichotomous items. A smaller excess in the far tail, traced to sparse score groups, keeps the family-wise rate at 6.8 to 8.6 percent for 20 dichotomous items. A parametric bootstrap removes it, apart from a slight excess at small n.
3. Infit with Westfall-Young is calibrated and detects more. It holds 4.2 to 4.4 percent family-wise under the null and detects at least as much as the S-X2 bootstrap and the df-corrected S-X2 in every cell, at nominal and at matched error rates. For subtle misfit and moderate n the difference is large.
4. S-X2 resists the cascade. When three items misfit at n \(\geq\) 1000, it rarely flags fitting items, while infit flags them in most datasets. Its advantage in recovering the right set of items is large where misfit is strong or moderate and n is large. The resistance belongs to the S-X2 statistic, since asymptotic S-X2 with Holm resists about as well as the bootstrap. The bootstrap’s contribution is calibration under the null, where asymptotic S-X2 with Holm is still at 5.8 to 8.6 percent.
5. RMSEA adds nothing beyond S-X2. A fixed threshold of .05 is unusable in both directions. A bootstrap cutoff makes RMSEA usable, but it then behaves like the S-X2 bootstrap.
Against the decision rule. The rule set before the run was that S-X2 is worth adding if its bootstrap version holds 5 percent under the null and, in a cell with \(\rho\) = 0.50 or 0.75, detects misfit infit misses or flags clearly fewer fitting items, without a comparable loss elsewhere. The first two parts are met. At \(\rho\) = 0.50 with three misfitting items, the S-X2 bootstrap flags fitting items in 3.5 against 39.5 percent of datasets at n = 1000 and 7.5 against 87 at n = 2000, with detection of 93.8 against 98 and 100 against 100. The third part is a judgement, since at \(\rho\) = 0.75 the S-X2 bootstrap detects much less than infit at every n up to 1000.
So S-X2 is neither a replacement for infit nor a better default. Its use is as a second opinion at large n: when infit flags many items, S-X2 separates the items that misfit from those that are flagged because others do. The bootstrap version holds the null and costs a refit per draw, about 25 to 40 seconds per analysis at B = 400 on one core for 20 items. Asymptotic S-X2 with the df corrected and Holm gives nearly the same second opinion at no cost, with a family-wise error rate of 6 to 9 percent instead of 5.

title: 2  Generalized S-X2 and conditional infit
text:
2.5 Scope and limits

The comparison uses dichotomous items only. The null study found S-X2 close to nominal for nine polytomous items after the df correction, so a polytomous comparison is the obvious next step.
One misfit mechanism, a second dimension. Other mechanisms, such as discrimination different from the Rasch model, may favour either method.
S-X2 is computed by mirt under MML with a normal latent distribution, which matches the data generation here and so favours it slightly.
The bootstrap uses df + 1 only to put S-X2 on a common scale across draws. Its reference does not depend on the df otherwise.

title: 3  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
text:
3.1 Purpose
The PCA/t-test protocol (Smith, 2002; Tennant & Pallant, 2006) splits a scale into two item sets from a principal component analysis of residuals, estimates a person location from each set, compares them per respondent with a t-test against 1.96, and refers the resulting proportion of significant tests to a 5% benchmark through a binomial confidence interval. Hagell (2014) showed that the conclusion depends on sample size and on which of five binomial interval methods is used, and argued the protocol should be read as ordinary hypothesis testing rather than as a definite test.
That leaves the reference proportion itself unexamined. This note shows that the 1.96 rule is not a 5% test, computes its exact size, and records what that does to the binomial step. The conclusion is that the choice of interval method is a second-order question about the shape of a distribution whose center is wrong by a factor of 1.3 to 3.7. The direction is uniform, so the protocol is biased toward declaring unidimensionality.

title: 3  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
section: 3.2 The statistic is the change index with subtests in place of occasions
text:
3.2 The statistic is the change index with subtests in place of occasions
The protocol computes
\[t = \frac{\hat\theta_A - \hat\theta_B}{\sqrt{SE(\hat\theta_A)^2 + SE(\hat\theta_B)^2}}\]
which is the Rasch change index of the RCI chapter with item subtests in place of occasions. Both mechanisms documented there (Section 4.2) carry over.
Self-normalisation. \(SE(\hat\theta_A)\) and \(SE(\hat\theta_B)\) are deterministic functions of the realised subtest scores, so the denominator is not independent of the numerator, both tails of the null are damped, and the critical value falls below 1.96. The “t” label is a misnomer for the same reason: a t denominator is independent of its numerator, which is the one property this denominator does not have.
Discreteness. With complete data each subtest score is sufficient, so \(\hat\theta_A\) and \(\hat\theta_B\) take only as many values as there are subtest scores and the null is a distribution over \((k_A+1) \times (k_B+1)\) cells.
Conditional independence, which is what makes the enumeration possible, also carries over, but it has a different standing in the two settings. In the change case it is an auxiliary assumption. The null there is that \(\theta\) did not move, and carry-over between two administrations of the same items can be present while \(\theta\) is fixed, so separate administration does not deliver conditional independence on its own. Section 4.11 covers what happens when it fails. Here the item sets are disjoint, so local independence gives \(P(r_A, r_B \mid \theta) = P(r_A \mid \theta)\,P(r_B \mid
\theta)\), and that statement is the null hypothesis rather than a condition attached to it. A failure is what the protocol exists to detect, so enumerating under it is the right move.
What the protocol cannot do is say which kind of failure it found. Marais & Andrich (2008) separate trait dependence, where a person parameter beyond \(\theta\) enters the responses, from response dependence, where the response to one item governs the response to another. Only the first is multidimensionality. Two locally dependent items in the same subtest reduce the information that subtest carries below what the model assumes, so \(SE_A\) understates the spread of \(\hat\theta_A\) and \(|t|\) is inflated, pushing the protocol toward rejection in the same way a second dimension would. That follows from the information rather than from anything measured here. It leaves the size calculations below untouched, since those hold under a null with no dependence of either kind, but it bears on what a rejection supports: that the item set fails local independence, not the stronger claim of multidimensionality that the procedure’s name carries.

title: 3  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
section: 3.3 Conditioning on the total score removes the latent distribution
text:
3.3 Conditioning on the total score removes the latent distribution
The RCI chapter enumerates the null at a set of person locations and pools over them, which makes the pooled critical value a property of the sample as well as the items. The subtest case admits a stronger construction. Under the Rasch model the conditional distribution of \(r_A\) given the total score \(r_A + r_B\) is free of \(\theta\), by the same sufficiency that underlies CML estimation:
\[P(r_A = a \mid r_A + r_B = r) = \frac{\gamma_A(a)\,\gamma_B(r-a)}{\gamma(r)}\]
So the null of \(t\) can be enumerated per total score with no latent distribution assumption and no plug-in person estimate. Numerically it is easier to evaluate \(P(r_A \mid \theta)P(r_B \mid \theta)\) at any convenient \(\theta\) and normalise within each total score, which gives the same ratio. Invariance is checked below rather than assumed.
Sufficiency and the recursion divide the work. Sufficiency is what makes the ratio free of \(\theta\), and it also fixes the value of \(t\) in every cell, since \(\hat\theta\) and \(SE\) are functions of the subtest score alone. Neither of those says what the \(\gamma\) terms are, and a quantile needs them. Computing them is what Lord-Wingersky does, as exact combinatorics rather than estimation.


Code
# Thresholds: k items, ncat response categories, locations spread over
# [-spread, spread]. Same constructor as the RCI chapter.
mk <- function(k, ncat, spread = 1.2) {
  lapply(seq(-spread, spread, length.out = k),
         function(b) b + seq(-0.9, 0.9, length.out = ncat - 1L))
}

# Lord-Wingersky: exact sum-score distribution given theta under a PCM
score_dist <- function(thr_list, theta) {
  d <- 1
  for (thr in thr_list) {
    p  <- easyRasch2:::.pcm_cat_probs(theta, thr)
    nd <- numeric(length(d) + length(p) - 1L)
    for (a in seq_along(d)) nd[a + seq_along(p) - 1L] <-
        nd[a + seq_along(p) - 1L] + d[a] * p
    d <- nd
  }
  d                                   # index = score + 1
}

# Score -> (theta, SE) lookup, WLE. The lookup RMscoreSE() builds.
lut <- function(thr_list) {
  steps <- vapply(thr_list, length, integer(1L))
  m <- vapply(0:sum(steps), function(r)
    easyRasch2:::.theta_wle(easyRasch2:::.score_pattern(r, steps),
                            thr_list, c(-10, 10)), numeric(2L))
  list(theta = m[1L, ], se = m[2L, ])
}

# The t grid and the raw logit-gap grid for one split
split_grid <- function(thr_all, idxA) {
  A <- thr_all[idxA]; B <- thr_all[-idxA]
  lA <- lut(A); lB <- lut(B)
  list(A = A, B = B, lA = lA, lB = lB,
       t = outer(seq_along(lA$theta), seq_along(lB$theta),
                 function(i, j) (lA$theta[i] - lB$theta[j]) /
                   sqrt(lA$se[i]^2 + lB$se[j]^2)),
       d = outer(seq_along(lA$theta), seq_along(lB$theta),
                 function(i, j) lA$theta[i] - lB$theta[j]))
}

# Null of t conditional on the total score. Free of theta.
cond_null <- function(g, theta_eval = 0) {
  dA <- score_dist(g$A, theta_eval); dB <- score_dist(g$B, theta_eval)
  maxA <- length(dA) - 1L; maxB <- length(dB) - 1L
  lapply(0:(maxA + maxB), function(r) {
    a <- max(0L, r - maxB):min(maxA, r)
    w <- dA[a + 1L] * dB[r - a + 1L]
    list(a = a, p = w / sum(w),
         t = g$t[cbind(a + 1L, r - a + 1L)],
         d = g$d[cbind(a + 1L, r - a + 1L)])
  })
}

alpha_by_r <- function(cn, crit = 1.96)
  vapply(cn, function(x) sum(x$p[abs(x$t) > crit]), numeric(1L))

gap_by_r <- function(cn) vapply(cn, function(x) sum(x$p * x$d), numeric(1L))

# Total-score distribution under a latent density, by quadrature
score_weights <- function(thr_all, mu = 0, sigma = 1.4, nq = 121L) {
  q <- seq(mu - 5 * sigma, mu + 5 * sigma, length.out = nq)
  w <- dnorm(q, mu, sigma); w <- w / sum(w)
  Reduce(`+`, Map(function(t, wt) wt * score_dist(thr_all, t), q, w))
}

# Pooled exact critical values achieving nominal alpha
crit_pooled <- function(cn, fr, alpha = 0.05) {
  tv <- unlist(lapply(cn, `[[`, "t"))
  pv <- unlist(Map(function(x, f) x$p * f, cn, fr))
  o <- order(tv); tv <- tv[o]; pv <- pv[o] / sum(pv)
  cw <- cumsum(pv)
  c(lower = tv[which(cw >= alpha / 2)[1L]],
    upper = tv[which(cw >= 1 - alpha / 2)[1L]])
}

# Exact Poisson-binomial distribution of the flagged count
pois_binom <- function(p) {
  d <- 1
  for (pi in p) d <- c(d * (1 - pi), 0) + c(0, d * pi)
  d                                   # index = count + 1
}

text:
3.4 Validation
Three anchors, following the discipline of the RCI chapter (Section 4.4): reproduce an identity to machine precision, and check the fast path against simulation.


Code
thr  <- mk(12, 4)
idxA <- seq(1, 12, by = 2)            # interleaved 6 / 6
g    <- split_grid(thr, idxA)

# Anchor 1: is the conditional null actually free of theta?
cn0 <- cond_null(g, 0); cnm <- cond_null(g, -2); cnp <- cond_null(g, 2.5)
dev1 <- max(vapply(seq_along(cn0), function(i)
  max(abs(cn0[[i]]$p - cnm[[i]]$p), abs(cn0[[i]]$p - cnp[[i]]$p)), numeric(1L)))

# Anchor 3: does the exact pooled critical value recover nominal alpha?
fr <- score_weights(thr, 0, 1.4); fr <- fr / sum(fr)
cp <- crit_pooled(cn0, fr, 0.05)
ach <- sum(vapply(seq_along(cn0), function(i) fr[i] *
  sum(cn0[[i]]$p[cn0[[i]]$t < cp[["lower"]] | cn0[[i]]$t > cp[["upper"]]]),
  numeric(1L)))


Anchor 1, theta-invariance. Evaluating the conditional distribution at \(\theta = -2\), \(0\) and \(2.5\) agrees to a maximum absolute difference of 1.9e-16. The construction is free of \(\theta\) rather than approximately so.
Anchor 2, against simulation. Four hundred thousand respondents on the 12-item scale, drawn from \(N(0, 1.4)\), scored and classified by the same 1.96 rule. Per-total-score \(\alpha\) agrees with the enumeration to a maximum absolute difference of 0.0040 against a Monte Carlo standard error of 0.0039. The simulation is not run at render time. It lives in scripts/ttest/ttest_protocol_exact_null.R.
Anchor 3, self-consistency. Feeding the exact pooled critical values back through the enumeration gives \(\alpha =\) 0.0492 against a nominal 0.05, the residual being discreteness.

text:
3.5 The 1.96 rule is not a 5% test


Code
run <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA, mu = 0, sigma = 1.4) {
  thr <- mk(k, ncat); g <- split_grid(thr, idxA); cn <- cond_null(g, 0)
  fr <- score_weights(thr, mu, sigma); fr <- fr / sum(fr)
  a <- alpha_by_r(cn, 1.96); gp <- gap_by_r(cn); cp <- crit_pooled(cn, fr, 0.05)
  nz <- a > 0
  data.frame(config = label, subtests = paste0(length(idxA), "/", k - length(idxA)),
             alpha = sum(fr * a), ratio = 0.05 / sum(fr * a),
             pct_zero = 100 * sum(fr[!nz]),
             lo = cp[["lower"]], hi = cp[["upper"]],
             asym = abs(cp[["lower"]]) - cp[["upper"]],
             gap = max(abs(gp[nz])), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

The true size of the 1.96 rule runs from 1.4% to 3.9%. It never reaches 5%, and at 40 items split 20/20 it is still short by a factor of 1.27. text:
3.6 A large share of respondents cannot be flagged at all
The last column above counts respondents for whom no attainable pair of subtest scores produces \(|t| > 1.96\). Their contribution to the significant count is zero with probability one, not 0.05. At 20 dichotomous items that is 44% of the sample and on an off-target polytomous scale 46%.

panel <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA) {
  g <- split_grid(mk(k, ncat), idxA)
  a <- alpha_by_r(cond_null(g, 0), 1.96)
  data.frame(label = label, r = seq_along(a) - 1L, alpha = a)
}
d_fig <- rbind(
  panel("20 items, 4 cat, 10/10", 20, 4, seq(1, 20, by = 2)),
  panel("12 items, 4 cat, 6/6",   12, 4, seq(1, 12, by = 2)),
  panel("20 items, 2 cat, 10/10", 20, 2, seq(1, 20, by = 2)))
d_fig$label <- factor(d_fig$label, levels = unique(d_fig$label))

ggplot(d_fig, aes(r, alpha)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_step(direction = "mid") +
  facet_wrap(~ label, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(x = "Total score across all items", y = "Exact type I error of 1.96") +
  theme_bw() + easyRasch2:::er2_axis_margins()








Figure 3.1: Exact size of the 1.96 rule by total score, under a perfectly unidimensional Rasch model. Weighted by a \(N(0, 1.4)\) latent density to give the sample means quoted in the text. The dashed line is the 5% the protocol assumes. Scores at both ends carry a size of zero because no attainable split of that total clears 1.96.





The sawtooth is discreteness. Adjacent total scores differ in how many attainable splits they have and where those splits fall relative to the cutoff, so the size of the test alternates rather than varying smoothly. The RCI chapter found the same structure in the conditional critical value, which formed an arch across the score range rather than a constant.
Figure 3.1 also shows that the conservatism is not a uniform shrinkage. Around the middle of the scale the size peaks at 0.062, 0.062 and 0.054 in the three panels, so the test is mildly anti-conservative there. Under the \(N(0, 1.4)\) weighting, 20%, 6% and 10% of respondents hold a total score whose size exceeds 0.05. The whole of the deficit comes from the ends, where attainable scores run out and the size falls to zero. Averaging over the score distribution is what the protocol does when it pools respondents into one proportion, and that average is what has to be compared with 5%, but a reader should know that the pooled figure is combining two opposite behaviours rather than describing a test that is uniformly too strict.

count_null <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA, n, mu = 0, sigma = 1.4) {
  thr <- mk(k, ncat); g <- split_grid(thr, idxA); cn <- cond_null(g, 0)

  a  <- alpha_by_r(cn, 1.96)
  nr <- round(n * fr); p_i <- rep(a, times = nr)
  d  <- pois_binom(p_i); cnt <- seq_along(d) - 1L; m <- length(p_i)
  mean_p <- sum(d * cnt) / m
  data.frame(config = label, n = m,
             mean_p = 100 * mean_p,
             q95    = 100 * cnt[which(cumsum(d) >= 0.95)[1L]] / m,
             p_over = sum(d[cnt / m > 0.05]),
             sd_pb  = sqrt(sum(d * cnt^2) - sum(d * cnt)^2),
             sd_bin = sqrt(m * mean_p * (1 - mean_p)),
             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}

At \(n = 1000\), observing more than 5% significant tests is an event of probability 0.0007, 0.0000, 0.0000 and 0.044 under a perfectly unidimensional model. The protocol treats 5% as the boundary of acceptability. The exact null puts it in the upper tail.
The binomial family is fine. Conditioning on the observed scores makes the count Poisson-binomial rather than binomial, since each respondent carries their own \(\alpha_r\). The last two columns show the two standard deviations agree to within a percent throughout. The heterogeneity in \(\alpha_r\) is too small relative to its mean to move the variance, because \(\mathrm{Var}_{\text{PB}} = n\bar\alpha - \sum \alpha_i^2\) differs from \(n\bar\alpha(1-\bar\alpha)\) by \(n\,\mathrm{Var}(\alpha_i)\), which is order \(10^{-4}\) against a mean of order \(10^{-2}\). Marginally, with person locations drawn iid from a latent density, the count is binomial in any case.
So the distributional shape Hagell (2014) investigates is not where the protocol goes wrong. All five of the interval methods compared there are being applied to roughly the right distribution and compared against the wrong number.

dist_one <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA, n = 500) {

  d <- pois_binom(p_i)
  data.frame(label = label, prop = 100 * (seq_along(d) - 1L) / length(p_i),

3.9 Extreme-score handling does not rescue it
The lookup above uses WLE, which is finite at extreme scores. Software using maximum likelihood person estimates has to drop respondents extreme on either subtest, so the check is whether that changes the size.

joint_w <- function(thr_all, idxA, mu = 0, sigma = 1.4, nq = 121L) {
  A <- thr_all[idxA]; B <- thr_all[-idxA]
  q <- seq(mu - 5 * sigma, mu + 5 * sigma, length.out = nq)
  w <- dnorm(q, mu, sigma); w <- w / sum(w)
  Reduce(`+`, Map(function(t, wt) wt * outer(score_dist(A, t), score_dist(B, t)),
                  q, w))
}
chk <- function(label, k, ncat, idxA, mu = 0) {
  thr <- mk(k, ncat); g <- split_grid(thr, idxA)
  W <- joint_w(thr, idxA, mu); W <- W / sum(W)
  sig <- abs(g$t) > 1.96
  keep <- matrix(TRUE, nrow(W), ncol(W))
  keep[c(1L, nrow(W)), ] <- FALSE; keep[, c(1L, ncol(W))] <- FALSE
  data.frame(config = label, all = sum(W * sig),
             pct_ex = 100 * (1 - sum(W[keep])),
             dropped = sum(W[keep] * sig[keep]) / sum(W[keep]))

title: 3  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
section: 3.10 What this changes about the protocol
text:
3.10 What this changes about the protocol
The protocol’s decision rule compares an observed proportion against 5%. That benchmark is too lenient by a factor of 1.3 to 3.7 across everything tried here, worst on dichotomous items and off-target samples, which are common in health measurement. The direction is uniform, so the protocol is biased toward declaring unidimensionality.
This also gives a mechanism for Hagell’s central finding (Hagell, 2014). Comparing against a benchmark that is too lenient shifts the whole power curve toward passing, so conclusions flipping with sample size is ordinary power behaviour against a biased reference rather than a pathology of the binomial interval. With the correct reference, mild multidimensionality would be rejected at appreciably smaller samples, and larger \(n\) would behave the way it does in any well posed test.
The constructive version is cheap. The enumeration needed to state the correct reference is the same machinery that produced it: one Lord-Wingersky recursion per subtest and one score-to-measure lookup, both of which the package already builds for RMscoreSE(). From that, either report the exact \(\bar\alpha\) and test the observed count against it, or replace 1.96 with the exact per-score critical values so that the 5% benchmark becomes true by construction. The second is closer to what users expect the protocol to mean and needs no change to how results are reported.

title: 3  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
section: 3.11 Not yet done: the split is chosen from the data
text:
3.11 Not yet done: the split is chosen from the data
Everything above conditions on a fixed, known split. The protocol chooses the split by principal component analysis of residuals, taking loadings above +0.3 and below -0.3, a cutoff whose rationale Hagell (2014) already calls unclear. That is a selection step, and the null conditional on a data-chosen contrast is not the null for a fixed one. The enumeration therefore understates the size of the protocol as practised.
The two errors run in opposite directions. Referring to 1.96, together with the respondents who cannot be flagged at all, pushes the realised proportion below 5% and makes the protocol too lenient. Selecting the most discrepant contrast pushes it up and makes the protocol too strict. Which dominates depends on item count, response categories, targeting and how unbalanced the split is, and nothing here settles it.
Settling it needs a parametric bootstrap of the whole pipeline: generate under the fitted unidimensional model, run the PCA, take the split, run the t-tests, count. That is the same shape as RMdimResidualPCACutoff() and the infit and Q3 cutoff work, and the exact component above would serve as its reference, which removes most of the noise from the comparison the way the exact RCI null did for the change study.
It is worth holding open that the two errors partly cancel. Existing simulation work reporting the protocol as well behaved under unidimensionality would be consistent with that, and a cancellation would not be stable across the conditions in the first table. I have not checked what Smith (2002) or Horton & Tennant (2010) report on this point, so that reading is a conjecture to verify against the sources rather than a finding of this note.

title: 3  An exact null for the PCA/t-test unidimensionality protocol
text:
3.12 Scope and limits

Complete data only, as in the RCI chapter (Section 4.12). Missing responses break sufficiency of a single subtest score, so the enumeration would run per missingness pattern.
Fixed split. See Section 3.11.
WLE with CML-style thresholds. RUMM2030’s person estimator may differ. It would move the centering column more than the size column, since dropping extremes barely changed the latter.
The latent density enters only through the weighting. The per-score sizes are free of it. Only the sample means and the count distributions depend on the assumed \(N(\mu, \sigma)\).
The 1.96 figure is taken as the rule in force. Software referring to a \(t\) distribution with finite degrees of freedom uses a slightly larger value, which makes the test more conservative, not less.

title: 4  An exact null for the Rasch change index
text:
4.1 Purpose
RMpersonChange() includes an option for critical = "simulate" rather than the conventional 1.96, because the Rasch change index
\[RCI = \frac{\hat\theta_2 - \hat\theta_1}{\sqrt{SE(\hat\theta_1)^2 + SE(\hat\theta_2)^2}}\]
is not standard normal under the null. The departure is largest on short scales and fades only slowly, so that even at 60 items with four response categories the critical value is still around 1.93. This note shows that the null does not need simulating at all: for complete data it can be enumerated exactly. It also records what the exact critical value does across test length, sample skew and targeting, and one consequence for the RCI as a statistic.

title: 4  An exact null for the Rasch change index
section: 4.2 Why the null is not N(0, 1)
text:
4.2 Why the null is not N(0, 1)
Two mechanisms, both weakening as test information grows.
Self-normalisation. \(SE(\hat\theta_1)\) and \(SE(\hat\theta_2)\) are deterministic functions of the realised scores, so the denominator is not independent of the numerator. A respondent who moves to an extreme score produces a large numerator and a large denominator together, and the ratio is damped. Both tails of the null are pulled in, so the critical value falls below 1.96. In a t-test the denominator is independent of the numerator. Here it is not, which is why the t reference does not help either.
Discreteness. With complete data the sum score is sufficient, so \(\hat\theta\) takes only as many values as there are scores and the null is discrete rather than continuous.

title: 4  An exact null for the Rasch change index
text:
4.6 Skew and targeting
Sample skew on its own barely moves the pooled critical value: the skewed and symmetric rows above agree to the third decimal in five of seven configurations. Targeting is what matters. Pushing the same skewed distribution 2.2 logits off target, so that 39.5% of respondents are at an extreme score at one occasion or the other, drops the critical value from 1.695 to 1.522. The mechanism is the self-normalisation in Section 4.2: a floor-bound sample is located primarily where the statistic is most heavily damped.
This also means the pooled critical value is a property of the sample as well as the items, which is worth stating wherever it is reported.
Recalibrating on each sample, which is what the function does, keeps the test close to its nominal level even when targeting is poor. Carrying a critical value across samples does not. Applying a value calibrated on a well-targeted sample to one sitting two logits off target gave a realised size of .028 against a nominal .05 on six items, where recalibrating on that sample held .042. Quote the value with the sample it came from, and recalibrate rather than reusing a published figure.

4.7 Can the sample dependence be removed?
Conditioning on the total score is what removed the latent distribution from the subtest problem of the PCA/t-test chapter (Section 3.3), and the same argument applies here. Under the null the two occasions are independent given \(\theta\) and use the same items, so
\[P(r_1 = a \mid r_1 + r_2 = s) = \frac{\gamma(a)\,\gamma(s-a)}{\gamma_2(s)}\]
where \(\gamma_2\) is the elementary symmetric function of the item set counted twice. The ratio is free of \(\theta\), verified to between 2.2e-16 and 3.9e-16 across four configurations including dichotomous and mixed-category scales. A per-respondent null is therefore available with no latent density and no plug-in person estimate.

4.8 A consequence for the RCI as a statistic
Because the denominator is a function of the same scores as the numerator, the RCI does not order respondents by how much they changed. A concrete pair from the six-item scale above:

The constructive version: since the critical value has to be computed from the item parameters anyway, the normalisation adds nothing that a location-specific threshold on the raw change would not. The same enumeration gives the null of \(\hat\theta_2 - \hat\theta_1\) directly, so a conditional critical change, in logits, is available at no extra cost and is monotone in what happened. That is the same object as a conditional minimal detectable change, and connects to the score-level MDC table parked as a possible sibling function.

section: 4.9 The no-change band in the figure
text:
4.9 The no-change band in the figure
The scatter plot of occasion 1 against occasion 2 draws a band covering the changes that would not be flagged. That band was built from a smooth approximation, half-width \(c \cdot \sqrt{2/I(\theta)}\), which places both occasions at the baseline location. The test does not do that. It uses \(SE(r_1)\) and \(SE(r_2)\) at two different scores.
On 300 respondents the two disagreed for 33 of them, 11 percent: 27 sat outside the drawn band without being flagged, and 6 sat inside it while flagged. The figure contradicted the table it accompanied.
The mechanism shows in the worst case. A respondent moving from \(\theta_1 =
1.23\) to \(\theta_2 = 3.62\) had a band built on \(SE_{diff} = 0.79\), because information is high at 1.23, while the test used 1.56, because the follow-up score is at the ceiling. The band was about half the width it should have been, in precisely the case the figure exists to display: a large change landing near a boundary.
The band is now built from the same lookup the test uses. For each attainable baseline score, the follow-up locations that would not be flagged are read off directly, so a point lies outside the band if and only if that respondent was flagged. Verified at zero disagreements out of 300 and pinned by a regression test. Because attainable scores are discrete the band is a step function, which also makes the discreteness visible rather than hiding it behind a smooth curve.

set.seed(1)
thr_demo <- mk(6, 4)
names(thr_demo) <- paste0("I", seq_along(thr_demo))

t1 <- as.data.frame(easyRasch2:::sim_partial_score(thr_demo, theta_demo))
t2 <- as.data.frame(easyRasch2:::sim_partial_score(thr_demo, theta_demo + 0.7))
colnames(t1) <- colnames(t2) <- names(thr_demo)

# Item parameters are estimated from the data here, as a reader would, so that
# this figure and the reliability output below share one calibration.
RMpersonChange(t1, t2, critical = "exact", output = "ggplot")

Its steps are the attainable scores, and it is widest away from the centre.

title: 4  An exact null for the Rasch change index
text:
4.11 Response dependence between occasions
Everything above assumes the two occasions are independent given \(\theta\). That is a conditional statement, and it is compatible with the two estimates being strongly correlated marginally, which they are. Both measure the same person, and that shared \(\theta\) is what makes their difference interpretable. The assumption concerns what is left once \(\theta\) is accounted for.
What it rules out is carry-over: a time-2 answer depending on the time-1 answer to the same item beyond what \(\theta\) explains. Administering the occasions separately does not deliver conditional independence on its own. Marais (2009) models the failure by shifting the time-2 difficulty of item \(j\) by \((1 - 2x_{j1})d\), so a positive response at time 1 makes that item easier at time 2 and a negative one makes it harder. Marais & Andrich (2008) separate this response dependence from trait dependence, which is multidimensionality. Only the second is a failure of unidimensionality, and the two call for different remedies.
This matters here in a way it does not for the PCA/t-test protocol (Section 3.2). There, conditional independence between the two item subsets is the null hypothesis, so a failure of it is what the test exists to detect. Here it is an auxiliary assumption: the null is that \(\theta\) did not change, and carry-over can be present while \(\theta\) is fixed.


Code
# Marais's model, generalised to polytomous items by shifting every threshold
# of item j by (1 - 2 * x_j1 / m_j) * d, which reduces to her dichotomous form
# when m_j = 1. Shifting all thresholds by s is the same as shifting theta by
# -s, so the shift is applied as an effective theta.
rpcm <- function(theta_eff, thr) {
  m <- length(thr)
  num <- matrix(0, length(theta_eff), m + 1L); cs <- cumsum(thr)
  for (k in seq_len(m)) num[, k + 1L] <- k * theta_eff - cs[k]
  num <- exp(num - apply(num, 1L, max))
  cp <- t(apply(num / rowSums(num), 1L, cumsum))
  max.col(cp >= runif(length(theta_eff)), ties.method = "first") - 1L
}

sim_pair <- function(thr_list, theta1, theta2, d = 0) {
  k <- length(thr_list); n <- length(theta1)
  mj <- vapply(thr_list, length, integer(1L))
  x1 <- vapply(seq_len(k), function(j) rpcm(theta1, thr_list[[j]]), integer(n))
  sh <- if (d == 0) matrix(0, n, k) else (1 - 2 * sweep(x1, 2L, mj, "/")) * d
  x2 <- vapply(seq_len(k), function(j)
          rpcm(theta2 - sh[, j], thr_list[[j]]), integer(n))
  list(t1 = x1, t2 = x2)
}

# Wider item spread than mk() above, following Marais's [-2.5, 2.5]
mk_wide <- function(k, ncat) {
  lapply(seq(-2.5, 2.5, length.out = k),
         function(b) b + seq(-0.9, 0.9, length.out = ncat - 1L))
}

score_lut <- function(thr_list) {
  steps <- vapply(thr_list, length, integer(1L))
  vapply(0:sum(steps), function(r)
    easyRasch2:::.theta_wle(easyRasch2:::.score_pattern(r, steps),
                            thr_list, c(-10, 10)), numeric(2L))[1L, ]
}


The mechanism is easiest to see with no true change at all. Holding every respondent at one location and generating both occasions from it, the mean observed change should be zero at every location, and is when \(d = 0\). Marais (2009) judged \(d = 0.5\) likely to pass unnoticed and \(d = 1\) possibly so, working from raw residual correlations and from differential item functioning by occasion, neither of which carried a calibrated reference. Against a simulation-based cutoff the lowest level she studied is caught in all 25 runs, with a clean zero under the null. Her conclusion about detectability reflects the diagnostics available at the time rather than a limit of the data.
Two details decide whether this works in practice. The statistic has to be centred on the cross-occasion pairs, not Yen-corrected against every pair. Subtracting the mean of all off-diagonal \(Q3\) mixes within-occasion pairs into the reference and costs power: at \(d = 0.5\) the two centrings detect in 96 and 100 percent of runs respectively, and the gap widens when real change is also present.

text:
4.12 Scope and limits

Complete data only. Missing data breaks sufficiency of a single sum score. Each distinct missingness pattern has its own score distribution and its own lookup, so the enumeration still works but per pattern.
null = "retest" needs quadrature. The occasion deviations are continuous, so the joint becomes a double integral over \(u_1, u_2\) rather than a pure sum. Still deterministic and cheap at, say, 21 nodes a side.
EAP is fine. On complete data an EAP estimate is also a function of the sum score.
Validated here for WLE with CML thresholds. Not yet checked against MML item parameters.
Conditional independence between occasions is assumed, not tested. The enumeration is correct under it and says nothing about carry-over. See Section 4.11, and screen for it before relying on a change verdict.

title: 4  An exact null for the Rasch change index
text:
4.13 Implemented
Shipped as critical = "exact", now the default in RMpersonChange(), in R/person_change_exact.R. Measured against a 4000-iteration simulation on the same data: critical values agree to within Monte Carlo error, p-values correlate at 0.9998, classifications are identical, and the exact path takes 0.08 s against 13.7 s. Incomplete data is enumerated within each missingness pattern, null = "retest" integrates the occasion deviations out by quadrature (they are independent, so the joint factorises and the retest null costs no more than the measurement null), and EAP is supported by holding the prior at the one the observed respondents were scored under.
Having an exact reference immediately paid for itself twice. It exposed a bug in the simulation path, which had been re-estimating the EAP prior from each null dataset rather than holding it at the observed one. That is now fixed, and the two paths agree to four decimals under EAP. It also supplied the lookup needed to fix the figure, described in Section 4.9.
It also removes the one real objection to conditional_crit = TRUE: a per-respondent critical value from simulation rests on sim_iter draws, roughly 25 of which land in each tail at alpha = .05, whereas \(P(r \mid \theta_i)\) is available per respondent for free.
It would also improve the planned simulation study, whose first aim is the realised Type I error of the simulated critical value. Much of the noise in that comparison disappears if the reference is exact.
